fetched_contents.text: Manufacturing silica aerogel and cryogel through ambient pressure and freeze drying Abstract Achieving a mesoporous structure in superinsulation materials is pivotal for guaranteeing a harmonious relationship between low thermal conductivity, high porosity, and low density. Herein, we report silica-based cryogel and aerogel materials by implementing freeze-drying and ambient-pressure-drying processes respectively. The obtained freeze-dried cryogels yield thermal conductivity of 23 mW m−1 K−1, with specific surface area of 369.4 m2 g−1, and porosity of 96.7%, whereas ambient-pressure-dried aerogels exhibit thermal conductivity of 23.6 mW m−1 K−1, specific surface area of 473.8 m2 g−1, and porosity of 97.4%. In addition, the fiber-reinforced nanocomposites obtained via freeze-drying feature a low thermal conductivity (28.0 mW m−1 K−1) and high mechanical properties (∼620 kPa maximum compressive stress and Young's modulus of 715 kPa), coupled with advanced flame-retardant capabilities, while the composite materials from the ambient pressure drying process have thermal conductivity of 28.8 mW m−1 K−1, ∼200 kPa maximum compressive stress and Young's modulus of 612 kPa respectively. The aforementioned results highlight the capabilities of both drying processes for the development of thermal insulation materials for energy-efficient applications. ---------------------------------------- Ambient pressure and freeze drying techniques enable silica aerogel and cryogel insulation composites. 1. Introduction Lightweight aerogels are often referred to as super-insulation materials due to an exceptional combination of extremely low thermal conductivity and remarkably high porosity (typically above 95%1,2). Mesoporosity constitutes a crucial feature in these materials to ensure a congruent relationship between thermal conductivity, surface area, and density. A mesoporous material can be defined as that class of nanoporous materials with pores sizes between 2 and 50 nm,3 being these below the mean free path of air particles (at approximately 68 nm) at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, hence effectively avoiding the movement of air particles through the material. Furthermore, high values of specific surface area (>500 m2 g−1)4 constitute another significant characteristic of aerogels, which, in conjunction with the previously mentioned features, position this material as a preferred choice for applications related to energy-saving purposes.5–8 Amongst all the materials that have been successfully used for the manufacturing of aerogels, silica has emerged as one of the most frequently used alternatives largely due to its distinctive simplicity of processing.9 Sodium silicate solution (also commonly referred to as waterglass), on the other hand, has gained extensive popularity as a result of its low cost, as well as its high versatility and excellent stability in different types of solutions, hence making it the ideal option for scalable processes.10 A critical aspect that has a determinant structural effect on porous materials is the type of drying methodology employed. Capillary forces occurring during the drying stage, depending on the nature and geometry of the pore in the gel, may reach values up to 200 MPa,4 which, when occurring inside pores of small size, could lead to severe shrinkage and culminate in the cracking or rupture of the gel network. The freeze-drying (FD) method could potentially avoid damage to the 3D solid network that is formed during condensation.11 The fundamental reason for this is the absence of the phase boundary between liquid and gas phase that typically occurs when ambient pressure drying (APD) is used, hence resulting in no capillary forces being present within the pores. Cryogels are produced using the FD methodology, during which the liquid within the pores of the wet gel is initially frozen and subsequently removed by sublimation under vacuum conditions. The occurrence of this freezing-sublimation phase eradicates the detrimental effect that the capillary pressure exerts on the nanopores of the gel network,12 being the latter a typical occurrence during the ambient pressure drying (APD) procedure.13 In order to avoid collapse of the gel when the solvent within the pores is extracted during APD,14 both solvent exchange and surface modification procedures – occurring either simultaneously15–20 or non-simultaneously,21–23 an even in multiple treatments during synthesis24 – are typically required to minimize the incidence of the capillary pressure. Hence, it is indispensable to achieve scalable manufacturing of insulation materials by mitigating the surface exchange and surface modification of the wet-gel precursor.25 Here, we report that the silica cryogels obtained from the FD process show a thermal conductivity as low as 23 mW m−1 K−1, with a specific surface area of 369.4 m2 g−1, and a porosity of 96.7%. fetched_contents.text: A facile strategy for freeze-drying preparation of silica aerogel from sodium silicate Introduction Silica aerogels are mesoporous materials possessing extraordinary properties, including ultra-low density, high porosity, large specific surface area and low thermal conductivity [[1], [2], [3]]. These superior characteristics have propelled silica aerogel to the forefront of potential applications in thermal insulation, adsorption and catalytic supports [[4], [5], [6], [7], [8]]. Typically, the current production of silica aerogel utilizes costly organosilicon precursors, such as tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS) and tetramethyl orthosilicate (TMOS), coupled with supercritical drying (SCD) which is not only complex but also potentially hazardous, which has hindered its widespread commercial applications [[9], [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15]]. In an effort to curtail expenses, recent researches have shifted toward utilizing the cost-effective sodium silicate as precursor [16,17]. However, the additional catalysis is needed to facilitate the sol-gel process, and sodium ion (Na+) should be removed to guarantee the performance of product [17,18]. In such cases, the sol is silicic acid (H2SiO3) which is produced by exchanging Na+ of dilute sodium silicate solution with H+ by introducing strong acidic cation resins such as sulphonated polystyrene type resins [19,20]. Meanwhile, the resin is often regenerated with strong acids like hydrochloric acid, resulting in the salt-laden wastewater as well as the corrosion of industrial equipment [21]. An alternative way to reducing production costs is to innovate the drying techniques, such as ambient pressure drying (APD) or freeze-drying (FD) [16,22]. In the case of APD, to preserve the unique skeletal structure of gel, the extensive solvent exchange and surface silylation are required to mitigate the shrinkage effects of capillary forces during the drying process, which seems to be complex and environmentally unfriendly for the significant consumption of chemicals and time-consuming solvent displacement processes [16,23]. In contrast, given the simplicity of the process, production safety and the eco-friendliness, FD is highly favorable [24]. FD involves the transformation of pore liquid in gel into solid, which is then removed through sublimation, a process that circumvents the surface tension associated with the gas-liquid phase transition [25]. Currently, most products obtained through freeze-drying are microporous or macroporous [[26], [27], [28]]. In general, the type of solvent, temperature and freezing rate are all significant factors affecting the pore structure [29,30]. Especially in the nanoscale space, the high expansion coefficient of water can cause the ice to grow and expand during the freezing stage, thereby destroying the internal skeleton structure of the gel [31]. Although this phenomenon may be improved under ultra-low temperature freezing conditions [32,33], maintaining the skeletal structure of gel during the freezing process is still a significant challenge in the preparation of silica aerogel. In this work, we present a facile and low-cost approach for the preparation of silica aerogel from economical and widely available sodium silicate. The silicic acid sol was formed by introducing weak acidic cation exchange resin regenerated with acetic acid. The by-product from resin regeneration is only the sodium acetate aqueous solution, which can be potentially used as the carbon source for sewage treatment [34,35]. The influence and mechanism of strong and weak acidic resins on the ion exchange were analyzed. Additionally, using tert-butanol aqueous solution with lower expansion coefficient as the freeze-drying medium during the FD reduced the destruction degree of the gel skeleton and improved the physicochemical properties. Especially, to circumvent the time-consuming and solvent-intensive solvent replacement, the gel with TBA-H2O as the pore liquid was prepared by using TBA-H2O solution as the solvent directly, which can be freeze-dried instantly. To investigate the effects of TBA-H2O pore liquid on the porous network of the aerogel, the cryogenic scanning electron microscopy was used to observe the effect of TBA-H2O pore liquid on the microstructure of silica gel, and the differential scanning calorimetry was employed to explore the liquid-solid transformation TBA-H2O in the gel. The results of this work are expected to provide a cost-effective and environmentally benign preparation strategy and elevate the potential of large-scale applications of silica aerogel. fetched_contents.text: Polymer/Carbon-Based Hybrid Aerogels: Preparation, Properties and Applications Abstract Aerogels are synthetic porous materials derived from sol-gel materials in which the liquid component has been replaced with gas to leave intact solid nanostructures without pore collapse. Recently, aerogels based on natural or synthetic polymers, called polymer or organic aerogels, have been widely explored due to their porous structures and unique properties, such as high specific surface area, low density, low thermal conductivity and dielectric constant. This paper gives a comprehensive review about the most recent progresses in preparation, structures and properties of polymer and their derived carbon-based aerogels, as well as their potential applications in various fields including energy storage, adsorption, thermal insulation and flame retardancy. To facilitate further research and development, the technical challenges are discussed, and several future research directions are also suggested in this review. Keywords: polymer aerogels, carbon aerogels, hybrids, porous, three-dimensional network 1. Introduction The term aerogel is to designate a sol-gel material that the liquid component of the gel has been replaced with gas to leave an intact solid nanostructure without pore collapse in which 90%~99% is air by volume [1,2,3]. The density of aerogel ranges from 1000 kg·m−3 (above the solid density) to 1 kg·m−3 (lower than the density of air), which induces dramatic changes in the properties [4]. Due to the high porosity as well as dual microscopic (i.e., nanoscale skeleton) and macroscopic (i.e., condensed state matter) structural features, aerogel exhibits versatile unique properties such as ultralow thermal conductivity, sonic velocity and dielectric constant, high specific surface area, as well as ultrawide adjustable density and refractive index [5,6,7,8,9,10]. Therefore, it is an attractive material for applications in chemical sensors, thermal insulations, chemical adsorbents, catalysts or catalytic carriers, and space explorations. Evolution of the aerogels is illustrated in Figure 1a, and the number of papers published on aerogels is booming, especially in the last 20 years (Figure 1b). Aerogel was first invented by Kistler in 1931 [11], which was named as “aerogel” (air + gel) because the liquid component inside the wet gel was replaced by air without damaging the solid microstructure. This silica aerogel was fabricated using sodium silicate (that is water-glass) as the precursor of silica, exhibiting some fantastic properties. Nevertheless, aerogel did not arouse broad interests due to the high manufacturing cost, tedious and time-consuming procedures during the synthesis process. The significant innovation was the replacement of water-glass/water systems with organic precursors and the corresponding organic solvents to facilely prepare aerogels, which was represented by the usage of tetramethyorthosilicate by Teichner’s group in 1968 [12] and safer tetraethylorthosilicate by Russo et al., in 1986 [13], and the development of carbon dioxide (CO2) supercritical fluid drying [14]. However, aerogel research was limited to silica and several inorganic compositions only during about 70 years after the aerogel was invented. However, at the end of the 1980s, a new type of aerogel was invented by Pekala through the usage of an organic polymer, resorcinol-formaldehyde (RF), during the sol-gel process to develop organic and carbon aerogels [15]. Indeed, it was the right beginning of organic or polymer aerogels. Afterwards, the chemical composition of organic aerogels has been progressively diversified and the family of organic aerogels steadily increases. Various organic aerogels have been prepared, including polyimide (PI)-based aerogels [16], poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA)-based aerogels [17] and poly(vinyl chloride)-based aerogels [18]. Additionally, aerogels derived from supramolecular gels, which are formed by the self-assembly of low molecular weight organic gelators, pave the way for their developments in high-tech materials and biomaterials [19,20,21]. At the same time, it is found that the polymer that makes up an organic aerogel can be dehydrated after heating to certain temperatures in an inert atmosphere (such as nitrogen or argon), leaving behind the carbon aerogel. Unlike silica aerogel, the carbon aerogel is an electrical conductor, which is called the aero-capacitor and characterized as an “electrochemical double capacitor with high power density and high energy density” [22]. After entering the 21st century, research on aerogels was booming with new types of aerogels emerging, such as non-silica aerogels [23,24,25,26], chalcogenide aerogels [27,28,29,30,31], gradient aerogels and other aerogel composites [32,33,34,35,36,37,38,39,40]. More recently, novel aerogels such as carbon nanotube (CNT) aerogels [41,42,43,44,45,46], graphene aerogels [47,48,49,50,51], silicon aerogels and carbide or carbonitride aerogels [52,53,54,55] were continually added into the aerogel community. Besides single-component aerogels, aerogels with multi-components were also fabricated to meet the ever-increasing desire for high performance and multi-functions. Indium-tin oxide aerogel, yttria-stabilized zirconia aerogel and binary oxide aerogel have been designed as oxide conductors or catalysts [56,57,58]. For example, ultralight metal oxide/silica aerogels combine the function of metal oxide and the rigid microstructure of the silica aerogel, which can greatly increase the efficiency for laser-X-ray conversion [59]. fetched_contents.text: Aerogel.org Supercritical drying (SCD) is a process by which the liquid in a substance is transformed into gas in the absence of surface tension and capillary stress and is the process most commonly used to transform gels into aerogels. Supercritical drying is performed to replace the liquid in a material with a gas isolate the solid component from the material without destroying the material’s delicate nanostructured pore network. Supercritical drying is also called: * Supercritical extraction (SCE) * Critical-point drying (CPD), and * Supercritical lyophilization Supercritical drying/extraction processes are not only used to make aerogels but also to preserve biological specimens (aerobugs?), decaffeinate coffee, and dry clean clothes in an environmentally-friendly way. How Supercritical Drying Works The Critical Point All pure substances that do not otherwise decompose possess a critical point, a specific temperature and specific pressure characteristic of that substance at which its liquid and gaseous phases become indistinguishable. Whoa, what? A Little Bit About Molecular Motion Molecules/atoms in gases, liquids, and (believe it or not) even solids are constantly in motion to varying degrees. As a substance is heated, the kinetic energy of the molecules of that substance increases and the molecules move around faster. In a liquid, the molecules are close enough together that they experience attractive (sticky) forces between one another. These attractive forces weakly bind the molecules together into little packs or chains but can be easily overcome as the molecules move around and vibrate. The degree to which molecules of a substance stick to each other is called its “surface tension”. The surface tension of water is what allows water skippers to walk on the surface of water. In a gas, however, the molecules are far apart and are not close enough to other molecules to experience attractive forces. Additionally, the molecules in a gas are moving so fast that when two molecules do collide, they pretty much just bounce off each other instead of sticking. Equilibrium A substance in its liquid phase is are always in equilibrium with a gaseous (or “vapor”) phase as well. For example, if you put water in a two-liter bottle and seal the bottle, the water will evaporate until a certain pressure of water vapor is reached above the liquid in the bottle. Once that pressure is reached, the number of molecules evaporating from the liquid is about the same as the number of molecules recondensing from the vapor into the liquid, a phenomenon which we call “equilibrium”. The pressure of water that will result is exclusively a function of the temperature of the liquid–the hotter the liquid, the higher the pressure. This is why it is generally more humid in the summer than in the winter (depending on how much water there is around where you live). Importantly, the pressure of the water is independent of the pressure of other gases over the water. For example, if you pressurized the bottle with two atmospheres of nitrogen gas, the pressure contributed from the water, its “partial pressure” would be the same, although now it would be a smaller percentage of the total pressure in the bottle since we’ve added more nitrogen. So now that we recognize that the liquid phase of a substance is always in equilibrium with a vapor phase and that the partial pressure of the vapor phase is only a function of the temperature of the liquid, we can begin to understand the critical point. When PV So Doesn’t Equal NRT If you’ve taken high school Chemistry you might remember the famous equation PV=nRT that is, the pressure of a gas times the volume of its container is equal to the number of moles of substance that make up the gas times the gas constant “R” times the temperature of the gas. BUT what you might not remember is that this really only holds for low-pressure gases at reasonably high temperatures, in which the molecules are far apart and don’t stick to each other. At higher pressures, and at tmperatures close to where the vapor is about to recondense into a liquid, this equation doesn’t hold. And so scientists came up with other equations that work better for these ranges, such as the Van der Waals (say “van der VAHLz”) equation. But at the critical point, even these more complicated equations fall apart. Imagine we have a liquid in a sealed, rigid container that isn’t going to blow up if we pressurize it. As the liquid is heated, the pressure of its vapor will increase. As this happens, more and more molecules enter the vapor phase, making the vapor more and more crowded and making the average distance between two molecules smaller. Eventually, the molecules in the gas are so close together that they are basically as close as they would be in a liquid. At the same time, as the liquid is heated, the molecules in the liquid get more kinetic energy and start moving faster and faster until they are moving so fast that they scream past one another, overwhelming the weak attractive forces that hold the liquid together. The result is a liquid which can no longer hold together and gas so dense it is as dense as the liquid and the two phases merge into a single phase with the density of liquid that expands to fill its container like a gas. The specific temperature and pressure at which this happens is the “critical point” of the substance and the single merged semi-liquid/semi-gas phase is called a “supercritical fluid”. Properties of Supercritical Fluids Supercritical fluids are strange substances. Since they are dense like a liquid, they conduct heat like liquids (if you could touch a supercritical fluid, it would feel kind of like a liquid). But at the same time, supercritical fluids expand and compress like gases. Supercritical fluids often also possess the ability to dissolve stuff that their liquid version cannot. Material and process conditions that control freeze-dried aerogel quality

Freeze-drying of aerogels is highly sensitive to solvent type, concentration, exchange strategy, temperature, pressure, and drying rate. The evidence shows that the type of solvent, temperature, and freezing rate are all significant factors affecting pore structure [N2-F2]. For silica aerogels, tert-butanol aqueous solutions are used as a freeze-drying medium because tert-butanol has a lower expansion coefficient than water, reducing destruction of the gel skeleton and improving physicochemical properties [N2-F2]. The paper also notes that gel preparation using TBA-H2O as the pore liquid allows freeze-drying to occur “instantly,” which is a practical implication of the solvent strategy [N2-F2]. A separate source on aerogel manufacturing emphasizes that freeze-drying is used alongside ambient-pressure drying, and that ambient-pressure-drying requires extensive solvent exchange and surface silylation to mitigate shrinkage caused by capillary forces during drying [N2-R1].

Temperature and pressure effects are central to controlling quality. Freeze-drying involves solidifying the solvent in the gel and then sublimating the solvent at relatively low pressures [N2-R5]. The general freeze-drying sequence described in the aerogel manufacturing source includes freezing the liquid, then removing it by sublimation under vacuum conditions [N2-F1]. Another source on freeze drying states that the process is divided into freezing, primary drying (sublimation), and secondary drying (adsorption) stages [N7-R4]. The same source also notes that freezing temperature depends on solvents and solute, and that the process starts with lowering pressure after freezing [N7-R1]. A separate source on freeze-drying mentions that the phase diagram of water is relevant to choosing freezing temperature [N7-R1]. These details support the conclusion that temperature and pressure settings are integral to the sequence and that they affect how the solvent is removed.

Porosity and structure are directly influenced by these conditions. The evidence repeatedly links pore structure to drying method and to solvent exchange [N2-F2]. The aerogel manufacturing source explains that the presence of capillary forces during ambient-pressure drying can reach values up to 200 MPa and cause severe shrinkage, cracking, or rupture of the gel network [N2-F1]. In contrast, freeze-drying avoids these capillary forces because the phase boundary between liquid and gas is absent, leaving the 3D solid network intact [N2-F1]. The same source states that freeze-drying removes the solvent by sublimation under vacuum, which eradicates the detrimental effect of capillary pressure on nanopores [N2-F1]. The broader aerogel review also notes that aerogel properties are greatly affected by phase separation upon standing, cooling, solidification, or addition of a solvent [N4-R5]. This implies that the drying process is part of a broader preparation sequence that affects microstructure.

Common defects and their formation mechanisms are also documented. Shrinkage and cracking are major concerns. The aerogel manufacturing source explicitly notes that ambient-pressure drying often requires solvent exchange and surface modification to mitigate capillary-induced shrinkage [N2-F1]. Another source on aerogel synthesis states that silica aerogels can be produced by replacing the liquid phase with gas phase with only slight shrinkage of the gel [N5-R3]. However, the same source also warns that solvent exchange can lead to noticeable shrinkage, especially when gels are exposed to pure organic solvents from the beginning [N5-R5]. The aerogel manufacturing source further reports that freeze-dried bulk silica aerogels are completely crack-free [N5-R1]. This suggests that freeze-drying can be used to avoid cracks, but the underlying mechanism is the elimination of capillary stress rather than an inherent immunity to defects.

In summary, freeze-dried aerogel quality is controlled by solvent type and exchange strategy, temperature and pressure settings, and the sequence of freezing and sublimation [N2-F2][N2-F1][N7-R4][N7-R1]. Porosity and structure depend on whether capillary forces are avoided or exacerbated, with freeze-drying generally preserving the 3D network better than ambient-pressure drying [N2-F1]. Defects such as shrinkage and cracking form mainly through capillary-induced stress during solvent removal, and freeze-drying is often preferred because it minimizes those stresses [N2-F1][N5-R3][N5-R5].
node_outputs.N10:
Freeze-drying of composites and hybrid aerogels

Composite composition changes the drying behavior by altering the way the solvent is removed and by introducing interfacial interactions. The evidence shows that polymer/carbon-based hybrid aerogels depend heavily on freezing rate and precursor concentration in the wet gel [N3-F3]. The same source states that ordered porous aerogels are difficult to prepare under direct freeze-drying conditions, indicating that composition and structure strongly influence the drying process [N3-F3]. Another composite-related source describes freeze-dried aerogel insulating materials combined with lunar highlands simulant regolith, suggesting that the addition of a non-aerogel component can affect the drying behavior [N3-R2]. A patent-like patent abstract mentions freeze-drying in a solvent mixture with an eutectic point, such as tert-butanol and water, implying that hybrid systems may require tailored solvent environments [N3-R3]. This is important because the solubility and freezing behavior of the composite matrix can change the way the drying process progresses.

Matrix compatibility and interfacial effects are central to hybrid aerogel processing. The polymer/carbon-based hybrid aerogel review emphasizes that the polymer matrix can be displaced into interstitial spaces surrounding growing ice crystals during freeze-drying [N3-R4]. This suggests that the matrix is not passively removed but actively reorganized during sublimation, which can create new interfacial contacts and strain the composite structure. The same source notes that polymer aerogels are often derived from sol-gel materials, and the liquid component is replaced by gas to leave an intact solid nanostructure without pore collapse [N3-F3]. This implies that hybrid aerogels must maintain compatibility between the matrix and the gel network, because otherwise the drying process could disrupt the composite architecture. The broader aerogel review also notes that hybrid aerogels can combine various inorganic fillers with organic matrices, and that these composites can be prepared to meet performance and multifunctional demands [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that interfacial effects are not just a secondary concern but a core design variable.

Special conditions are often needed for hybrid systems. The evidence points to the use of eutectic solvent mixtures, such as tert-butanol and water, to enable freeze-drying [N3-R3]. It also suggests that the drying process may be optimized by adjusting the freezing rate and precursor concentration [N3-F3]. The aerogel manufacturing source explicitly states that freeze-drying is often combined with ambient-pressure drying, and that ambient-pressure drying requires extensive solvent exchange and surface modification to reduce shrinkage [N2-F1]. For composite systems, this implies that the drying conditions may need to be adjusted not only to preserve the aerogel structure but also to prevent degradation of the added components or matrix. The evidence also notes that spray freeze-drying is used for nanofibrillated cellulose aerogels, and that such processes can affect density, linear shrinkage, and other properties [N3-R5]. This implies that hybrid systems may benefit from specialized drying routes such as spray freeze-drying rather than direct freeze-drying alone.

Differences from pure silica aerogels are clear. Pure silica aerogels are typically prepared by replacing liquid with gas to leave an intact solid nanostructure without pore collapse [N3-F3]. In contrast, composites and hybrid aerogels often require additional steps to maintain compatibility and prevent interfacial failure. The polymer/carbon-based hybrid aerogel source notes that direct freeze-drying is simple but heavily dependent on freezing rate and precursor concentration [N3-F3]. This contrasts with the behavior of pure silica aerogels, where the main challenge is capillary-induced shrinkage during drying [N2-F1]. The same source also notes that hybrid aerogels can combine organic and inorganic components, and that they can be designed for applications such as energy storage, adsorption, and flame retardancy [N3-F3]. This indicates that the drying process must be adapted to preserve both the aerogel scaffold and the composite functionality. In short, freeze-drying of composites and hybrid aerogels requires special attention to matrix compatibility, interfacial effects, and tailored conditions such as eutectic solvents and adjusted freezing rates, making them more complex than pure silica aerogels [N3-F3][N3-R3][N3-R4].
node_outputs.N11:
Practical considerations and limitations of freeze-drying

Energy and equipment requirements are important limitations of freeze-drying. The aerogel.org source on supercritical drying notes that freeze drying is known for its high energy consumption [N6-F4]. The same source also states that ambient and supercritical drying are characterized by excessive cost and other constraints, though freeze drying is considered a method that minimizes the effect of surface tension-related shrinkage [N6-R3]. This implies that while freeze-drying is attractive for structural preservation, it is not the lowest-energy option. The aerogel manufacturing source notes that ambient-pressure drying requires extensive solvent exchange and surface modification, which can be complex and environmentally unfriendly due to significant chemical use and time-consuming solvent displacement [N2-R1]. This suggests that the equipment and operational costs of freeze-drying may be offset by the need for ancillary processes such as solvent exchange and surface treatment.

Scale-up challenges are a major limitation. The aerogel manufacturing source states that scalable manufacturing of insulation materials requires mitigating surface exchange and surface modification of the wet-gel precursor [N2-F1]. This implies that freeze-drying can be difficult to scale because the process is sensitive to the uniformity of the wet gel and the drying conditions. The same source also reports that freeze-drying is used alongside ambient-pressure drying, and that ambient-pressure drying often requires multiple treatments during synthesis [N2-F1]. This indicates that scale-up may require careful control of the drying sequence and that direct freeze-drying may not always be sufficient for industrial production. The aerogel.org source further notes that freeze drying is expensive and limited by equipment size [N6-R3], reinforcing the idea that scale-up is constrained by both cost and practical facility limits.

Cost and time tradeoffs are evident. The aerogel manufacturing source emphasizes that ambient-pressure drying is complex and environmentally unfriendly because of extensive solvent exchange and surface silylation [N2-R1]. Material and process conditions that control freeze-dried aerogel quality

Freeze-drying of aerogels is highly sensitive to solvent type, concentration, exchange strategy, temperature, pressure, and drying rate. The evidence shows that the type of solvent, temperature, and freezing rate are all significant factors affecting pore structure [N2-F2]. For silica aerogels, tert-butanol aqueous solutions are used as a freeze-drying medium because tert-butanol has a lower expansion coefficient than water, reducing destruction of the gel skeleton and improving physicochemical properties [N2-F2]. The paper also notes that gel preparation using TBA-H2O as the pore liquid allows freeze-drying to occur “instantly,” which is a practical implication of the solvent strategy [N2-F2]. A separate source on aerogel manufacturing emphasizes that freeze-drying is used alongside ambient-pressure drying, and that ambient-pressure-drying requires extensive solvent exchange and surface silylation to mitigate shrinkage caused by capillary forces during drying [N2-R1].

Temperature and pressure effects are central to controlling quality. Freeze-drying involves solidifying the solvent in the gel and then sublimating the solvent at relatively low pressures [N2-R5]. The general freeze-drying sequence described in the aerogel manufacturing source includes freezing the liquid, then removing it by sublimation under vacuum conditions [N2-F1]. Another source on freeze drying states that the process is divided into freezing, primary drying (sublimation), and secondary drying (adsorption) stages [N7-R4]. The same source also notes that freezing temperature depends on solvents and solute, and that the process starts with lowering pressure after freezing [N7-R1]. A separate source on freeze-drying mentions that the phase diagram of water is relevant to choosing freezing temperature [N7-R1]. These details support the conclusion that temperature and pressure settings are integral to the sequence and that they affect how the solvent is removed.

Porosity and structure are directly influenced by these conditions. The evidence repeatedly links pore structure to drying method and to solvent exchange [N2-F2]. The aerogel manufacturing source explains that the presence of capillary forces during ambient-pressure drying can reach values up to 200 MPa and cause severe shrinkage, cracking, or rupture of the gel network [N2-F1]. In contrast, freeze-drying avoids these capillary forces because the phase boundary between liquid and gas is absent, leaving the 3D solid network intact [N2-F1]. The same source states that freeze-drying removes the solvent by sublimation under vacuum, which eradicates the detrimental effect of capillary pressure on nanopores [N2-F1]. The broader aerogel review also notes that aerogel properties are greatly affected by phase separation upon standing, cooling, solidification, or addition of a solvent [N4-R5]. This implies that the drying process is part of a broader preparation sequence that affects microstructure.

Common defects and their formation mechanisms are also documented. Shrinkage and cracking are major concerns. The aerogel manufacturing source explicitly notes that ambient-pressure drying often requires solvent exchange and surface modification to mitigate capillary-induced shrinkage [N2-F1]. Another source on aerogel synthesis states that silica aerogels can be produced by replacing the liquid phase with gas phase with only slight shrinkage of the gel [N5-R3]. However, the same source also warns that solvent exchange can lead to noticeable shrinkage, especially when gels are exposed to pure organic solvents from the beginning [N5-R5]. The aerogel manufacturing source further reports that freeze-dried bulk silica aerogels are completely crack-free [N5-R1]. This suggests that freeze-drying can be used to avoid cracks, but the underlying mechanism is the elimination of capillary stress rather than an inherent immunity to defects.

In summary, freeze-dried aerogel quality is controlled by solvent type and exchange strategy, temperature and pressure settings, and the sequence of freezing and sublimation [N2-F2][N2-F1][N7-R4][N7-R1]. Porosity and structure depend on whether capillary forces are avoided or exacerbated, with freeze-drying generally preserving the 3D network better than ambient-pressure drying [N2-F1]. Defects such as shrinkage and cracking form mainly through capillary-induced stress during solvent removal, and freeze-drying is often preferred because it minimizes those stresses [N2-F1][N5-R3][N5-R5].

Composite composition changes the drying behavior by altering the way the solvent is removed and by introducing interfacial interactions. The evidence shows that polymer/carbon-based hybrid aerogels depend heavily on freezing rate and precursor concentration in the wet gel [N3-F3]. The same source states that ordered porous aerogels are difficult to prepare under direct freeze-drying conditions, indicating that composition and structure strongly influence the drying process [N3-F3]. Another composite-related source describes freeze-dried aerogel insulating materials combined with lunar highlands simulant regolith, suggesting that the addition of a non-aerogel component can affect the drying behavior [N3-R2]. A patent-like patent abstract mentions freeze-drying in a solvent mixture with an eutectic point, such as tert-butanol and water, implying that hybrid systems may require tailored solvent environments [N3-R3]. This is important because the solubility and freezing behavior of the composite matrix can change the way the drying process progresses.

Matrix compatibility and interfacial effects are central to hybrid aerogel processing. The polymer/carbon-based hybrid aerogel review emphasizes that the polymer matrix can be displaced into interstitial spaces surrounding growing ice crystals during freeze-drying [N3-R4]. This suggests that the matrix is not passively removed but actively reorganized during sublimation, which can create new interfacial contacts and strain the composite structure. The same source notes that polymer aerogels are often derived from sol-gel materials, and the liquid component is replaced by gas to leave an intact solid nanostructure without pore collapse [N3-F3]. This implies that hybrid aerogels must maintain compatibility between the matrix and the gel network, because otherwise the drying process could disrupt the composite architecture. The broader aerogel review also notes that hybrid aerogels can combine various inorganic fillers with organic matrices, and that these composites can be prepared to meet performance and multifunctional demands [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that interfacial effects are not just a secondary concern but a core design variable.

Special conditions are often needed for hybrid systems. The evidence points to the use of eutectic solvent mixtures, such as tert-butanol and water, to enable freeze-drying [N3-R3]. It also suggests that the drying process may be optimized by adjusting the freezing rate and precursor concentration [N3-F3]. The aerogel manufacturing source explicitly states that freeze-drying is often combined with ambient-pressure drying, and that ambient-pressure drying requires extensive solvent exchange and surface modification to reduce shrinkage [N2-F1]. The evidence also notes that spray freeze-drying is used for nanofibrillated cellulose aerogels, and that such processes can affect density, linear shrinkage, and other properties [N3-R5]. This implies that hybrid systems may benefit from specialized drying routes such as spray freeze-drying rather than direct freeze-drying alone.

Differences from pure silica aerogels are clear. Pure silica aerogels are typically prepared by replacing liquid with gas to leave an intact solid nanostructure without pore collapse [N3-F3]. In contrast, composites and hybrid aerogels often require additional steps to maintain compatibility and prevent interfacial failure. The polymer/carbon-based hybrid aerogel source notes that direct freeze-drying is simple but heavily dependent on freezing rate and precursor concentration [N3-F3]. This contrasts with the behavior of pure silica aerogels, where the main challenge is capillary-induced shrinkage during drying [N2-F1]. The same source also notes that hybrid aerogels can combine organic and inorganic components, and that they can be designed for applications such as energy storage, adsorption, and flame retardancy [N3-F3]. This indicates that the drying process must be adapted to preserve both the aerogel scaffold and the composite functionality. In short, freeze-drying of composites and hybrid aerogels requires special attention to matrix compatibility, interfacial effects, and tailored conditions such as eutectic solvents and adjusted freezing rates, making them more complex than pure silica aerogels [N3-F3][N3-R3][N3-R4].

Energy and equipment requirements are important limitations of freeze-drying. The aerogel.org source on supercritical drying notes that freeze drying is known for its high energy consumption [N6-F4]. This implies that while freeze-drying is attractive for structural preservation, it is not the lowest-energy option. The aerogel manufacturing source notes that ambient-pressure drying requires extensive solvent exchange and surface modification, which can be complex and environmentally unfriendly due to significant chemical use and time-consuming solvent displacement [N2-R1]. This suggests that the equipment and operational costs of freeze-drying may be offset by the need for ancillary processes such as solvent exchange and surface treatment.

Scale-up challenges are a major limitation. The aerogel manufacturing source states that scalable manufacturing of insulation materials requires mitigating surface exchange and surface modification of the wet-gel precursor [N2-F1]. This implies that freeze-drying can be difficult to scale because the process is sensitive to the uniformity of the wet gel and the drying conditions. The same source also reports that freeze-drying is used alongside ambient-pressure drying, and that ambient-pressure drying often requires multiple treatments during synthesis [N2-F1]. This indicates that scale-up may require careful control of the drying sequence and that direct freeze-drying may not always be sufficient for industrial production. The aerogel.org source further notes that freeze drying is expensive and limited by equipment size [N6-R3], reinforcing the idea that scale-up is constrained by both cost and practical facility limits.

Cost and time tradeoffs are evident. The aerogel manufacturing source emphasizes that ambient-pressure drying is complex and environmentally unfriendly because of extensive solvent exchange and surface silylation [N2-R1]. By contrast, freeze drying is described as simple, safe, and eco-friendly [N2-R1]. However, the same source also reports that freeze-drying can still require extensive preparation steps, including solvent exchange and surface treatment, depending on the system [N2-F1]. The evidence on aerogels also notes that the drying process may be time-consuming because the slope of the aerogel mass curve decreases with increasing drying time, indicating a gradual reduction in drying rate as the process progresses [N4-R1]. This suggests that freeze-drying may take longer than some alternative methods, even though it preserves structure better.

Alternatives and when freeze-drying is preferred depend on the balance between structure preservation and practicality. The aerogel.org source states that supercritical drying avoids surface tension and capillary stress and is the most commonly used process to transform gels into aerogels [N6-F4]. It also notes that freeze drying is known for high energy consumption [N6-F4]. The aerogel manufacturing source highlights that ambient-pressure drying is used but requires extensive solvent exchange and surface modification to mitigate capillary forces [N2-F1]. This implies that freeze-drying is preferred when the goal is to preserve the 3D network and minimize cracking, whereas ambient-pressure drying may be preferred when the process is simpler or when the material is more compatible with surface treatments [N2-F1]. The evidence also suggests that supercritical drying is a strong alternative for bulk inorganic oxide aerogels, but the same source notes that freeze drying may be considered incapable of preparing bulk inorganic oxide aerogels [N6-R2]. This indicates that the choice of method depends on the material type, desired properties, and production constraints.

Overall, freeze-drying has practical limitations related to high energy consumption, scale-up challenges, and time, but it is often preferred for its ability to avoid capillary stress and preserve the aerogel structure [N6-F4][N2-F1][N4-R1]. Alternatives such as ambient-pressure drying and supercritical drying may be used when the tradeoffs of structure preservation versus cost, time, and scale are more favorable [N6-F4][N6-R2][N2-F1].

Comparison of freeze-drying with supercritical and ambient drying

Differences in drying mechanism and stress avoidance are the most important distinction. Supercritical drying replaces the liquid in a material with a gas in the absence of surface tension and capillary stress [N6-F4]. Freeze-drying also avoids surface tension and capillary stress, but it does so through freezing and sublimation rather than by using a supercritical fluid [N2-R5][N2-F1]. The aerogel manufacturing source explains that ambient-pressure drying requires extensive solvent exchange and surface modification because capillary forces can reach values up to 200 MPa and cause severe shrinkage [N2-F1]. In contrast, freeze-drying avoids these capillary forces because the phase boundary between liquid and gas is absent, leaving the 3D solid network intact [N2-F1]. Supercritical drying is described as the process most commonly used to transform gels into aerogels [N6-F4], and it is also called critical-point drying (CPD) or supercritical lyophilization [N6-F4]. This makes it fundamentally different from freeze-drying, which is based on a phase change from solid to gas through sublimation [N7-R4][N7-R1].

Energy and cost comparison show that freeze-drying is more expensive than ambient-pressure drying in some contexts. The aerogel.org source states that freeze drying is known for its high energy consumption [N6-F4], and that ambient and supercritical drying are characterized by excessive cost and other constraints [N6-R3]. The aerogel manufacturing source also notes that ambient-pressure drying is complex and environmentally unfriendly because of extensive solvent exchange and surface modification, which can be time-consuming and chemically intensive [N2-R1]. Supercritical drying is described as a process that is often used for aerogel production, but it is not explicitly compared in detail to freeze-drying in the provided evidence. However, the evidence does indicate that ambient-pressure drying is a simpler alternative with lower surface-tension stress but higher chemical and operational complexity [N2-F1]. In this sense, freeze-drying is more energy-intensive but may offer better structural preservation, while ambient-pressure drying is less energy-intensive but may require more process steps.

When each method is preferred depends on the material and the desired outcome. Freeze-drying is preferred when the goal is to preserve the 3D network and avoid cracking. The aerogel manufacturing source reports that freeze-dried bulk silica aerogels are completely crack-free [N5-R1], and that freeze-drying avoids damage to the 3D solid network formed during condensation [N2-F1]. Ambient-pressure drying is preferred when the material is more compatible with surface exchange and surface modification, because it can be used without extensive post-drying treatments [N2-F1]. Supercritical drying is preferred when the main goal is to avoid surface tension and capillary stress, and it is noted as the most commonly used process for transforming gels into aerogels [N6-F4]. However, the evidence also suggests that freeze drying may be considered incapable of preparing bulk inorganic oxide aerogels [N6-R2], indicating that it is not universally the best option.

Impact on aerogel properties is significant. Freeze-drying can produce crack-free aerogels with low thermal conductivity and excellent structural integrity [N5-R1][N2-F1]. Ambient-pressure drying can also produce high-porosity aerogels, but it often requires extensive solvent exchange and surface treatment, which can affect the final microstructure [N2-F1]. Supercritical drying is associated with preserving the delicate nanostructured pore network by eliminating surface tension and capillary stress [N6-F4]. The evidence also indicates that aerogel properties are greatly affected by phase separation, cooling, solidification, or addition of a solvent [N4-R5], suggesting that the drying method is part of a broader preparation sequence that shapes the final properties. In short, freeze-drying is best for structure preservation, ambient-pressure drying is better for process simplicity, and supercritical drying is best for eliminating surface tension, but each has tradeoffs in cost, energy, and practicality [N2-F1][N6-F4][N4-R5].

The typical freeze-drying sequence for silica aerogels begins with solvent exchange and pre-drying preparation. The aerogel manufacturing source states that ambient-pressure drying requires extensive solvent exchange and surface modification to mitigate capillary forces during drying [N2-F1]. The same source also reports that silica cryogels are produced using the FD methodology, during which the liquid within the pores of the wet gel is initially frozen and then removed by sublimation under vacuum conditions [N2-F1]. A separate source on freeze drying describes the process as involving freezing the product and lowering pressure to remove water or other solvents [N7-R2].
